ekl1: Are your joints very flexible but often painful, prone to sprains, or are you often tired? What is joint hypermobility, what does the Beighton score show, and which exercises protect the joints?
ekl3: Have you been “bendy” since childhood, but your joints often ache, your ankle sprains easily and you tire quickly? In joint hypermobility, the ligaments that support the joints are looser. For many people it causes no problems at all; when it does, the most effective approach is to strengthen the joints with the muscles around them and spread the day’s load evenly.

ekl30: Six exercises to protect the joints
ekl31: Start with few repetitions, slowly and with control; do the movements in the middle of the joint’s range, not pushing to the end. If pain or tiredness is clearly worse the next day, reduce the amount, then build up again slowly.
ekl32: Stand upright in front of the worktop, holding on lightly with one hand if needed. Lift one foot; keep the standing knee slightly bent rather than locked back. As it gets easier, try without holding on or with your eyes closed. It improves joint position sense and balance.
ekl33: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet on the floor. Squeeze your buttocks to lift your hips, making a straight line from your shoulders to your knees; do not arch your lower back too much. Hold for 3–5 seconds and lower slowly.
ekl34: Kneel on your hands and knees; keep your elbows slightly bent rather than locked. Stretch one arm forward and the opposite leg back; do not let your lower back sag or your hips rotate. Hold for 5 seconds and switch.
ekl35: Stand with your back against a wall and your feet half a step in front of it. Keep your knees pointing the same way as your toes, not caving in. Slowly squat a little and come back up; do not lock your knees back as you straighten.
ekl36: Stand or sit upright. Without lifting your shoulders towards your ears, draw your shoulder blades back and slightly down towards each other. Hold for 5 seconds and relax. It helps the muscles around the shoulder support the joint.

ekl41: No. Many people with flexible joints have no problems at all. But in some people, flexibility comes with pain, frequent sprains or dislocations and tiredness; in that case it is called joint hypermobility syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder.
ekl43: It is a simple 9-point examination doctors use to assess joint flexibility: bending the little finger back more than 90 degrees, touching the thumb to the forearm, the elbow and the knee bending backwards more than 10 degrees (one point each for right and left), and placing the palms flat on the floor with the knees straight (one point). In adults, a score of 4 or more is usually regarded as hypermobile. It is not a self-diagnosis test; the diagnosis is made by a doctor.
ekl45: If your joints already move too far, stretches that push them to their limit are generally not recommended. The aim is not to increase flexibility but to strengthen and protect the joints with the muscles around them. It is also recommended to avoid repeating the same movement for a long time.
ekl46: Has exercise been proven to help?
ekl47: The evidence is limited but encouraging. In the few studies available, strength, balance and endurance exercise reduced pain and improved strength; but it is not yet known which type of exercise is best. That is why programmes are tailored to the person and increased gradually.
